newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu declares a victory over Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu declares a victory over Jerusalem.

text.p: Defying international and Palestinian protests, a buoyant Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has declared a victory in the battle for Jerusalem.

But a day after Israel approved the building of thousands of Jewish homes in Arab East Jerusalem, Israeli media reported on Thursday police were likely to recommend charging three central figures in a probe of alleged government corruption.

"I know you came to strengthen me, but I came to strengthen you. I feel very strong." Netanyahu told a meeting of activists of his Likud party as Israel Radio said police would question him again soon and caution him about self-incrimination.

"I have one characteristic, you know, I love challenges. But most of all, I love to win. And we are winning. We set goals for ourselves and we have achieved another one of them," he said, referring to the settlement project.

Labour Minister Eli Ishai on Thursday signed the building permit that would pave the way for bulldozers to start rolling on Jabal Abu Ghneim, a hilltop of pine trees between Jerusalem and PLO-ruled Bethlehem. It is called Har Homa by Israel. Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and views all of the city as its capital. The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) wants East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

"I estimate building of the new neighbourhood of Har Homa will begin in the coming two weeks," a spokesman quoted Ishai as saying at a signing ceremony attended by civil servants who planned the project.
Jerusalem's Israeli mayor, Ehud Olmert, said a parallel project to build some 3,000 Arab homes could begin in a week.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat deplored the Israeli moves but gave no hint of what action he intended to take.

"This is a big breaching to what had been agreed upon and it is against the United Nations resolutions and also against the American letter of guarantees and against all the agreements that had been signed," he told reporters in the West Bank.

Israel deployed 500 extra police and troops in Jerusalem to forestall Palestinian protests. Israeli security chiefs met on Thursday to plan further measures ahead of Moslem prayers on Friday, police said.
On Thursday, a "national dialogue" conference grouping Palestinian Islamist and secular factions in the West Bank town of Nablus issued a final communique fiercely criticising Israel.
"Confronting settlements and resisting Judaisation is a legal act...peace cannot be achieved with the continuation of occupation," it said.
But Palestinian and Israeli analysts believe Arafat will not openly call for confrontation, particularly ahead of a scheduled meeting next week with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday criticised the building project and said any action that impeded future peace negotiations was unhelpful.

Netanyahu also faced pressure at home. Israel radio and television stations said police were likely to seek charges against Justice Minister Tsahi Hanegbi, Shas party leader Arye Deri and Netanyahu adviser Avigdor Lieberman.
All have denied any wrongdoing in the short-lived appointment last month of Jerusalem lawyer and Likud activist Roni Bar-On as attorney-general.

Police launched an investigation five weeks ago after Israel Television reported that Deri, on trial for corruption for the last three years, coerced the government to appoint Bar-On in the hope of winning a plea bargain.

Deri's party belongs to Netanyahu's coalition and legal experts say bowing to political blackmail would fall under the crime of breach of public trust. Several cabinet ministers have said the government would collapse if the charges proved true.
